questions.reasoning: 247 CMR 6.03 (Suitability of Applicant, Licensee, and Interest Holder; Mass. Register #1546, 4/25/2025). Every one of the eleven listed factors is framed as 'An applicant, licensee, or interest holder', so the factors reach a minority interest holder as well as the applicant company (A). The chapeau states the Board 'may determine an applicant or licensee is not suitable ... and that it would not be in the interest of public health, safety, and welfare to issue a license' (E). 6.03(10) lists a professional licence that 'was the subject of proceedings resulting in the discipline, suspension, denial, or revocation of the license or registration' (D). B is false because 6.03(5) and 6.03(11) expressly list consent agreements resolving a complaint. C is false because 6.03(4) through (6) reach any pharmacy, healthcare facility or other entity registered by the FDA or DEA, which is not limited to Massachusetts, and 6.03(10)-(11) reach any professional licence.

247 CMR 6.11(1): 'At least 14 days prior to the transfer of ownership of a licensed pharmacy, the licensee shall notify the Board of the proposed transfer of ownership. The outgoing licensee shall comply with 247 CMR 6.12 and 247 CMR 6.13 pertaining to closing a pharmacy and distributing controlled substances.' The buyer's duty under 6.11(2)-(3) is separate and does not discharge the seller's own notice obligation, so the seller's position is unsound (A). B is wrong because surrender of the original licence is a post-closure submission under 6.13(6), not a precondition. C, D and E each rest on the buyer's filing standing in for the seller's, which 6.11(1) forecloses.

247 CMR 6.14(2). Subparagraph (a) requires the transferor on the date of transfer to inventory 'all controlled substances in Schedules II through V and all controlled substances in Schedule VI required to be reported to the prescription monitoring program' (C). Subparagraph (f) provides that 'the transferor pharmacy may not possess any controlled substances after the date of transfer' (E), which also defeats A. B is wrong because 6.14(2)(d) requires the attestation to be filed with the Board within ten days of the transfer, not 30. D is wrong because 6.14(2)(b) requires both the transferor's and the transferee's Managers of Record to sign the inventory report.

247 CMR 6.17(4): 'A provisional license may not be renewed or extended.' 247 CMR 6.17(2)(c) makes the provisional licence valid only until 'one year has passed since the Board issued the provisional license'. Together these give E. A and B invent an extension power the regulation withholds; C misstates a discretionary conversion power as mandatory; D is wrong because 6.17(3) permits conversion only 'when the Board has determined the pharmacy is in full compliance', which has not occurred.

247 CMR 7.02(6): 'Changes in any information in 247 CMR 7.02(5) shall be submitted to the Board in writing within 30 days after such change.' The warehouse address and the contact/responsible person for each facility are 7.02(5)(a) and (c) information, so both changes go to the Board within 30 days rather than at renewal. On the conviction, 247 CMR 7.02(7)(b) lists 'any felony convictions of the applicant or licensee under federal, state, or local laws' as a minimum factor the Board shall consider, without any requirement that the offence relate to drugs; 7.02(7)(a) separately covers drug-related convictions. So the compliance officer is wrong on both points, and C is correct. D is wrong on the conviction limb and B is wrong on the reporting limb.

247 CMR 11.05: 'A separate controlled substance registration shall be required at each principal place of business where the licensee or registrant manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances.' So the existing registration does not cover the new warehouse. 247 CMR 11.06(3): 'The controlled substance registration issued to a wholesale druggist shall be valid for one year beginning on December 1st of each year' (renewal by 30 November under 11.07(2)(c)); the two-year even-year cycle in 11.06(1)-(2) applies to pharmacies and outsourcing facilities, not wholesale druggists. Counsel is therefore wrong on both points (D). 247 CMR 7.02(4) points the same way for the Board wholesale licence: a licence is required for each location.

247 CMR 13.02 defines radiopharmaceutical service as 'the counting, dispensing, labeling, and delivery of radiopharmaceuticals; participating in radiopharmaceutical selection and radiopharmaceutical utilization reviews; properly and safely storing and distributing radiopharmaceuticals; maintaining radiopharmaceutical quality assurance; advising on therapeutic values, hazards, and use of radiopharmaceuticals; and offering or performing those acts, services, operations or transactions necessary in the conduct, operation, management and control of radiopharmaceutical services within a nuclear pharmacy.' A and E track the first and fifth limbs verbatim. B (operating imaging equipment) and C (interpreting images) appear nowhere in the definition and are the practice of nuclear medicine, not nuclear pharmacy. D is wrong because the definition reaches participation in selection and utilization review, not prescribing, which under M.G.L. c. 94C is a practitioner function.

247 CMR 21.03(3): 'An entity with a provisional outsourcing facility registration may compound sterile drug preparations, but may not distribute or dispense a sterile drug preparation within or outside the Commonwealth until it has been inspected by the FDA and received a Massachusetts outsourcing facility registration.' That is exactly E: compounding is permitted, supply is not. B is defeated by the express words 'within or outside the Commonwealth'. D is the mirror-image error, since compounding is permitted. A and C treat the provisional registration as a full operating authority, which 21.03(3) denies.

105 CMR 700.008 (Mass. Register #1514, 2/2/2024): 'A registrant shall report the theft, loss or suspected tampering of any controlled substances to the Drug Control Program within the Department within 24 hours of discovery of such theft, loss or suspected tampering, by completing and submitting the form provided or approved by the Drug Control Program for such purpose.' The trigger is discovery (Monday), the recipient is the Drug Control Program within the Department of Public Health, and suspected tampering is itself reportable, so no confirmed loss is needed. That gives A and defeats B (wrong body), C (wrong trigger date), D and E (both defer or dispense with the report).

247 CMR 9.16(7) (12/6/24; Mass. Register #1536): 'The computerized pharmacy system shall provide for the immediate retrieval of information necessary for the pharmacist to identify previously dispensed drugs at the time the prescription is presented for dispensing.' That duty is unqualified, so C is correct and A and D fail. The 'reasonable effort' qualifier in the next sentence attaches only to obtaining, recording and maintaining the listed profile content, not to the retrieval capability, so B misreads the provision. 247 CMR 9.16(8): 'The requirements in 247 CMR 9.16 do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies' (E).

M.G.L. c. 112, s. 24B1/2(a), definition of 'collaborative practice agreement': 'Each collaborative practice agreement shall be subject to review and renewal on a biennial basis.' At twenty-six months without review the agreement is outside its currency period, so D is correct. A, B and C would let an unreviewed agreement run on; the statute attaches currency to the biennial review itself, not to whether circumstances have changed, whether a review is diarised, or whether the physician has terminated it. E overstates the consequence: the statute imposes no reporting duty for acts taken in month 25.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A: 'A pharmacist shall offer to counsel any person who presents a new prescription for filling. Such offer shall be made either by face to face communication between the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and the patient, or by telephone, except when the patient's needs or availability require an alternative method of counseling.' The method is therefore prescribed, not open (defeating A and D), the telephone is available (defeating C), and the deaf patient is the paradigm of the statutory exception permitting an alternative method rather than a reason to withhold counselling (defeating E).

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21A, final paragraph: 'The provisions of this section shall not apply to any drug dispensed to an inpatient at a hospital or nursing home, except to the extent required by regulations promulgated by the Federal Health Care Financing Administration pursuant to the provisions of 42 USC 1396r-8.' B states the carve-out and C states its express federal proviso. A contradicts the carve-out. D is wrong because the carve-out is keyed to the drug being dispensed to an inpatient, not to the identity of the pharmacy, so the lobby outpatient window remains within the section. E is wrong because the carve-out names 'a hospital or nursing home'.

247 CMR 9.04(3): 'A licensee shall ensure the label affixed to a prescription drug container or package is clearly printed by a computerized pharmacy system. In the event of printing or equipment failure, a prescription label may be legibly handwritten or typed during an emergency period.' Saturday's printer failure is precisely an equipment failure creating an emergency period, so handwriting was permitted. By Monday the printer had been repaired, so no failure subsisted and a long queue is not an equipment failure, so Monday's handwriting was not permitted. That is A. B ignores the emergency-period precondition, C ignores the express exception, D invents a prior-approval requirement, and E treats workload as an equipment failure.

247 CMR 9.04(7): 'Whenever a prescription drug has been distributed solely under a generic name, the dispensing pharmacist shall record the NDC number in the computerized pharmacy system. In the event an NDC number does not exist, the pharmacist shall record the name of the manufacturer, or, if the manufacturer's name is not available, the name of the distributor, packer, or repacker.' The provision is a strict cascade. With no NDC but the manufacturer's name available on the carton, the manufacturer's name is what must be recorded, the repacker being reached only if the manufacturer's name is unavailable. That is D, and it defeats A (not a free choice), B and C (repacker is subordinate, and nothing requires both), and E.

247 CMR 9.04(8): 'A pharmacy intern, or certified pharmacy technician who has the approval of the pharmacist on duty may receive new prescriptions over the telephone from a prescriber or authorized agent.' The restrictive clause qualifies the certified technician, so an intern may take the call (C) and a certified technician may do so with the on-duty pharmacist's approval (E). A is wrong because the provision expressly extends beyond the pharmacist. B and D are wrong because the class is closed to interns and certified technicians; a general employee or an uncertified technician is outside it, and after-the-fact verification does not cure that.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a): a written or electronic prescription for a Schedule II controlled substance 'shall become invalid 30 days after the date of issuance.' Thirty days after 1 March is 31 March, so 31 March is the day on which the prescription becomes invalid and 30 March is the last day on which it remains within date; equivalently the 30-day window runs 1 to 30 March inclusive. That is A. B would keep the prescription valid on 31 March, contradicting the statutory moment of invalidity. C adds a thirty-first day, D subtracts a day by excluding both ends, and E is wrong because the stem stipulates a thirty-day window, so the schedule is not in issue. I record a reservation: no Massachusetts statute I could retrieve fixes the counting convention in terms (M.G.L. c. 4, s. 9 addresses only Sundays and legal holidays), and 105 CMR 721.055(B)(2) uses the different formulation 'not later than 30 days after the Prescription issue date', so the A/B distinction is finer than the authority cleanly resolves.

Board of Registration in Pharmacy Policy 2021-02, Shared Pharmacy Service Models Including Central Fill, Remote Processing, and Telepharmacy (adopted 2/19/21, revised 4/7/22), IV.a and IV.b.ii: central fill is available only between Board-licensed retail pharmacies, and 'any central fill pharmacy dispensing medications into, within, or from Massachusetts to participating pharmacies must be licensed in Massachusetts.' 247 CMR 6.02(4) is to the same effect for any out-of-State pharmacy shipping controlled substances (which in Massachusetts include Schedule VI) into the Commonwealth, and 247 CMR 9.20 requires a non-resident pharmacy to comply with all Massachusetts law when filling or shipping into Massachusetts. So the answer is 'No', which excludes A and B: the receiving pharmacist's inspection of the finished vials does not cure processing by an unlicensed facility, and 247 CMR 9.04(1) makes a licensed pharmacist responsible for final dispensing process validation. Among the three 'No' options C is the only tenable one; D is too absolute because central fill between Board-licensed pharmacies is expressly permitted, and E reduces the defect to a documentation point. I record a reservation that C's stated condition (verification by a Massachusetts licensed pharmacist) is not the operative requirement, which is the central fill pharmacy's own Massachusetts licensure.

105 CMR 700.012(A)(3): a pharmacy 'must require that a customer identifier is presented whenever a controlled substance in Schedules II through V, or an additional drug is dispensed', and may dispense without reviewing the customer identifier only if the pharmacy has reason to believe non-dispensing 'would result in a serious hardship for the ultimate user or agent of the ultimate user, and documents the reason; and the ultimate user or agent of the ultimate user prints their name and address on the reverse side of the prescription and signs their name thereto, or in the case of an electronic prescription, provides an electronic signature; and the pharmacy provides to the Department those informational fields required by the Department.' The conditions are cumulative, so documentation (B) and the agent's printed name, address and signature (D) are both required, and A fails because belief alone is not enough. C is wrong because familiarity is not an exception. E is wrong because the requirement runs to Schedules II through V and to substances the Department has classified as additional drugs, not to Schedule VI on the same terms.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21, first paragraph: the pharmacist filling a written, electronic or oral prescription for a controlled substance shall affix 'a label showing the date of filling, the pharmacy name and address, the filling pharmacist's initials, the serial number of the prescription, the name of the patient, unless it is a veterinary prescription, the name of the prescribing practitioner, the name of the controlled substance, directions for use and cautionary statements, if any, contained in such prescription or required by law, and if the controlled substance is dispensed as tablets or capsules the number of same in such container.' That yields B, C, D (the drug is dispensed as capsules) and E. A is wrong: the label must carry the prescribing practitioner's name, not a registration number. The practitioner's registration number belongs on the prescription under s. 22(a) and in the pharmacist's written record of an oral prescription under s. 20(a), not on the container label.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21, second paragraph: 'Upon the request of an elderly person, as defined in section fourteen of chapter nineteen A or a person visually impaired, directions on the label affixed by the pharmacist to a container of a prescription drug shall be typed in a print size allowing no more than ten characters per inch.' The duty is request-activated, so the eighty-two year old who says nothing triggers nothing, and the second patient's request as a visually impaired person triggers the ten-characters-per-inch requirement. That is A. B ignores the request precondition, C ignores the provision altogether, D adds a prescriber's order the statute does not require, and E extends the requirement beyond the directions, whereas the statute reaches 'directions on the label' only.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20. Subsection (a) required the pharmacist to reduce the oral prescription to writing immediately, which she did, so C is wrong. Subsection (b): 'If the prescribing practitioner is not known to the pharmacist, he shall make a reasonable effort to determine that the oral authorization came from a registered practitioner' - the caller was unknown to her and no verification was attempted. Subsection (c): the practitioner 'shall cause an electronic prescription for the prescribed controlled substance to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy within 2 days', the seven-day written alternative being available only where the practitioner holds a commissioner exception under s. 23(h), which this prescriber does not. Eight days have passed. Both defects are live, which is E. A denies any defect, B would bar oral prescriptions that s. 20 contemplates, and D imposes a pre-dispensing writing requirement the section does not.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(b): 'Written prescriptions for a controlled substance in schedule II shall be kept in a separate file.' Section 23(c): 'The pharmacist filling a written or electronic prescription for a controlled substance in Schedule II shall endorse his own signature on the face thereof.' Both are missing here: the prescription was filed with the Schedule III and IV prescriptions, and only initials on the label were recorded rather than the pharmacist's signature on the face of the prescription. That is E. A and C treat the label initials or the filing as sufficient, B ignores s. 23(c), and D invents a second pharmacist's countersignature that s. 23 does not require. 247 CMR 9.16(2) points the same way on segregation.

105 CMR 700.005(B)(2): 'No registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation or has had their registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation at any time.' The words 'at any time' are decisive and defeat A, since eleven incident-free years do not run out the disqualification. B fails because the prohibition is on employing the person as an agent or employee, without a proximity qualifier, and 700.005(B) in any event reaches employees 'who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled'. C and E invent cures (notification, a vouching registrant) that the regulation does not provide. The answer is D.

247 CMR 6.13. Paragraphs (1), (2) and (3) each require written notice to the Board by certified mail at least 14 days before the intended closure, covering respectively the Massachusetts pharmacy, the non-resident pharmacy and the sterile and institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, so A is correct for all three. 6.13(3) requires the sterile compounding pharmacy to notify the Board 'of the identity of the pharmacy licensed by the Board that is suitable and available to provide continuity of care to the closing pharmacy's patients', which gives both C and E. 6.13(7) provides that '247 CMR 6.13(3) and 247 CMR 6.13(4) are not required for institutional sterile compounding pharmacies', and 6.13(4) is the Notice to Patients duty, so D is correct. B is the only false statement: the closing words of 6.13(6) provide that 'the provisions in 247 CMR 6.13(6) shall not apply to non-resident pharmacies', and 6.13(6)(a) is the post-closure submission of original licences.

247 CMR 6.16: 'A pharmacy licensed by the Board shall apply to the Board for approval to relocate to a new address prior to relocating and may not relocate until it receives approval from the Board. A pharmacy shall submit an application at least 90 days prior to its desired date of relocation, unless otherwise approved by the Board.' Both limbs of B are therefore right, and a move of two doors along is still a relocation to a new address. A substitutes notice for approval and a week for 90 days, C uses the 14-day period that belongs to closure and transfer provisions, D dispenses with prior approval altogether, and E treats relocation as terminating the licence, which 6.16 does not.

247 CMR 6.15(1): a Drug Store pharmacy 'shall apply to the Board for approval to remodel or to change the configuration or square footage of the pharmacy and may not commence any construction work or remodeling until it receives approval from the Board.' Filing on the morning work begins therefore breaches the prior-approval requirement. 247 CMR 6.15(3)(a) requires 'blueprints or equivalent architectural drawings depicting the pharmacy layout, prescription area, and counseling area', so drawings of the prescription area alone are incomplete. Both defects are captured by A. B treats approval as retrospective, C invents an architect certification for a Drug Store pharmacy (certified blueprints are required of compounding pharmacies under 6.15(4)(a)), D substitutes a fresh licence, and E sends the application to the wrong body.

247 CMR 6.15(2): a sterile compounding pharmacy 'shall apply to the Board for approval to remodel or to change the configuration or square footage of the pharmacy prior to moving, adding, modifying, removing, or replacing any secondary engineering control and may not move, add, modify, remove, or replace any secondary engineering control until it receives approval from the Board.' 'Replacing' is expressly within the trigger and no like-for-like exception appears, so B is correct and A and E fail. 247 CMR 6.15(4)(a) requires 'certified blueprints depicting compounding area(s) and the location and ISO classification of each primary and secondary engineering control, and placement of containment hood(s), as applicable', so D is correct and C fails, ordinary layout drawings under 6.15(3)(a) being insufficient for a sterile compounding pharmacy.

247 CMR 6.10. Subparagraph (2)(a) requires an attestation confirming an inventory 'of all controlled substances in Schedules II through V and controlled substances in Schedule VI required to be reported to the prescription monitoring program' and provides that 'the attestation shall be signed by the outgoing Manager of Record and the proposed incoming Manager of Record', which gives A and B. 6.10(1) provides that 'the Board may require the proposed pharmacist Manager of Record to appear before the Board prior to approving or denying an application' (E). C is wrong because a staff pharmacist may sign only where the outgoing Manager of Record is unavailable due to death, serious illness or termination, and then only if the Board is notified of the reason at the time of submission; convenience is not a ground. D is wrong because 6.10(2)(b) requires the original Drug Store Pharmacy licence, not a certified copy.

247 CMR 6.12 (Notifications): 'A licensee shall notify the Board, within 14 days, in writing, any change in the name under which the pharmacy operates, accompanied by appropriate authorizing documentation.' A trading-name change is squarely within that provision even though the licence holder, premises and ownership are unchanged, so C is correct and A and B fail. D borrows a 90-day period that belongs to relocation under 6.16 and misdescribes it as a notice period. E is wrong because 6.12 requires notification, not a fresh licence application. I note that 247 CMR 11.08(1)(b) and (2) separately provide that a controlled substance registration terminates on a change of name and require written notice to the Board within 14 days, which is consistent with C.

source_acquisition_method: All Massachusetts regulations were downloaded as official mass.gov document PDFs with curl (https://www.mass.gov/doc/<slug>/download), one of which required an explicit Referer header, and their text was extracted locally with PyMuPDF; every downloaded file was checked for a %PDF signature so that mass.gov block pages could not be mistaken for regulation text, and each extracted text was checked for its Mass. Register or MA REG currency stamp. General Laws sections were retrieved from malegislature.gov section pages over HTTPS with a browser User-Agent and parsed from the paragraph elements following the skipTo anchor. Web search was used only to locate official mass.gov and malegislature.gov URLs; no search snippet, secondary compilation, commercial summary or LLM output was relied on for any substantive proposition. Work was carried out in a private scratch directory after an unrelated concurrent process was observed overwriting a file in the shared scratchpad; every input was thereafter re-derived from the content-addressed git blob or from a freshly downloaded and signature-checked file.
